<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README, this project is an open‐source email verification tool called “check‑if‑email‑exists.” Its main purpose is to determine whether an email address is valid and reachable without sending an email by checking various aspects (syntax, DNS/MX records, SMTP, disposable status, etc.). The project is organized into multiple interacting components that together deliver several interfaces: a HTTP backend, a CLI tool, and a Rust library for programmatic inclusion in other projects.

Here’s how you can draw a high‑level, detailed system design diagram tailored for this project:

1. Identify the main components:
   • HTTP Backend Service (backend): This module (under the “backend” directory) exposes HTTP endpoints (with distinct versions, such as v0 and v1 under the “src/http” folders) for email verification requests. It uses migration scripts (in the “migrations” subdirectory) and configuration files (like backend_config.toml) indicating potential database use or internal state management.
   • CLI Application (cli): A command‑line interface that directly invokes the email verification functions provided by the underlying Rust library. Represent this as a separate interface component.
   • Core Library (core): Contains the central email verification logic. It includes modules for SMTP, syntax, DNS, miscellaneous helper functions, and integration with third‑party services (for example, checking against “Have I Been Pwned?”). This forms the backbone of the email-check functionality.
   • SQS Worker (sqs): There is a dedicated “sqs” directory with its own Dockerfile and Terraform file (main.tf). This implies there’s an additional microservice component likely handling asynchronous tasks (perhaps processing email verification tasks from a message queue).
   • Infrastructure & CI/CD: Directories like “.github/workflows,” “docker-compose.yaml,” “Makefile,” and “ci” scripts indicate that the project uses Docker containers, CI pipelines, and possibly orchestration for deployment. Although not a runtime component per se, it should be noted as part of the supporting architecture.
   • External Dependencies: Mark external services like:
       - DNS servers (for MX record lookup)
       - SMTP servers (for testing connectivity and deliverability)
       - External API calls to services like “Have I Been Pwned?”
       - (Optionally) Proxy servers, if used via the HTTP backend for email testing.
       
2. Define the relationships and data flow:
   • User Interfaces: Represent two main client entry points – one via HTTP requests (to the backend) and one via the CLI.
   • In the backend component, incoming HTTP requests (for example, a POST to /v0/check_email) trigger internal calls to the Core Library to perform the individual email verifications.
   • The CLI directly calls into the Core Library, starting the email verification process.
   • The SQS worker might be shown as a background task that could be triggered by the backend or directly polling a message queue for asynchronous processing.
   • External interactions: Draw arrows from the Core Library to external mail servers (SMTP, DNS queries) and third‑party APIs (e.g., for data breach checks).
  
3. Highlight key architectural patterns and design principles:
   • Separation of concerns: The HTTP backend, CLI, and core logic are clearly separated. The core library encapsulates all business logic so that it can be reused across interfaces.
   • Microservices/Modular design: With separate directories (“backend,” “cli,” “core,” “sqs”), the project is designed as modular components which may be deployed independently.
   • Containerization & CI/CD: The presence of Dockerfiles, docker-compose configurations, and GitHub workflows suggests that container-based deployment and automated testing are critical aspects. This should be highlighted as part of the operational architecture.
  
4. Include relevant technologies, frameworks, or libraries:
   • Rust: The project is written in Rust, with Cargo managing dependencies.
   • Docker: Used for containerizing the HTTP backend and SQS worker.
   • CI/CD tools: GitHub Actions workflows used for deployment and pull request checks.
   • Database (if applicable): The “migrations” folder indicates some kind of persistent store (possibly PostgreSQL) even if it is only for managing state or logging verification requests.
  
5. Guidelines for tailoring the diagram to this project type:
   • Since this is a tool that can work as a full‑service API (HTTP backend) as well as a CLI tool, ensure you distinctly represent both client interfaces.
   • Emphasize the central Core Library as a reusable component that both the backend and CLI rely on.
   • If portraying asynchronous processing (via SQS), indicate the decoupled nature of the SQS worker, using an arrow to signify that tasks are enqueued from the backend and processed separately.
   • Show any external services as separate nodes outside the main system (e.g., SMTP servers, DNS resolvers, third‑party APIs) with directional arrows to/from the Core Library.
  
6. Elements to include in the diagram:
   • Clearly labeled boxes for each component: “HTTP Backend”, “CLI Tool”, “Core Library”, “SQS Worker”, “Database/Migrations”, and “External Services”.
   • Directional arrows to indicate data flow:
       - From end‑users or API clients to the “HTTP Backend” 
       - From the “HTTP Backend” and “CLI” to the “Core Library”
       - From the “Core Library” to external services (DNS, SMTP, HaveIBeenPwned API)
       - From the “HTTP Backend” to the “SQS Worker” (if it pushes jobs)
   • Use different shapes or colors to differentiate between application components, infrastructure elements (such as Docker/CI/CD), and external systems.
   • Optionally, include annotations to note key configurations (e.g., use of Docker, CI workflows, migration scripts for setting up a database).
  
By following these detailed instructions, you will create a comprehensive system design diagram that accurately captures the multi‑faceted architecture of the “check‑if‑email‑exists” project, illustrating all components, their responsibilities, and how they interact both internally and with external services.
</explanation>
